prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: These, Wealthy, And

outputs.L1:
These water birds flew from the minds of fishermen  
And became fishing peons.  
Wealthy sailors watched as darters emerged once more  
To spread their drenched wings in the sun,  
And marked them as emblems for spinnakers.  

Painters and ornithologists studied darters  
Until they became black-feathered arrows  
That pierced the souls of their creators.  
These birds rode the surf of bitter laughter  
And wiped out on a zoo’s concrete Key Largo.  

To imitate darters, lovers tore off their clothes  
And plunged into the swiftness of estuaries.  
Down the water column, they entered brackish hell,  
Their hair transformed into iridescent plumage,  
Ruffled by memories of Earth’s human atmosphere.  

We can experience the lives of these feathered beings  
By flexing our particular despairs each morning.  
At evening, we take in the news as best we can.  
Late at night, we gaze upon dead bodies of water  
And almost perceive those wet wings working the tide.
outputs.L2:
From fishermen’s imaginations, the aquatic birds took flight,  
Only to serve as laborers of the catch.  
Affluent mariners saw anhingas surface once more,  
Opening their soaked wings beneath the sunlight,  
And adopted their shapes as symbols on spinnaker sails.  

Artists and bird scholars observed them so intently  
That the darters turned into dark-plumed projectiles,  
Striking deep into the spirits of those who envisioned them.  
Carried on breakers of caustic laughter,  
They crashed against a zoo’s cement version of Key Largo.  

Seeking to resemble the birds, lovers stripped bare  
And dove into the racing currents of estuaries.  
They descended through the water into a brackish underworld,  
Where their hair changed into shimmering feathers,  
Stirred by recollections of Earth’s human air.  

Each morning, by exercising our own distinct sorrows,  
We may enter the existence of these winged creatures.  
At dusk, we absorb the news however we are able.  
Far into the night, we contemplate lifeless bodies of water  
And nearly discern those drenched wings laboring with the tide.
outputs.L3:
Water birds first emerge from fishermen’s imaginations, shaped into obedient servants whose bodies, instincts, and movements are harnessed to the work of fishing. Later, wealthy sailors appropriate the image of the darter: its broad, sun-drenched wings become an emblem emblazoned across their spinnakers, transforming a living bird into a symbol of freedom, prestige, and mastery over wind and water.

Artists and ornithologists reinterpret the birds in more unsettling ways. In their hands, darters become symbolic black-feathered arrows—creatures that not only invite observation but also pierce the souls of those who portray, study, or attempt to possess them. Lovers, too, are drawn into this imaginative world. Imitating the birds, they cast off their clothes, plunge into estuaries, and envision themselves transformed into iridescent, feathered beings, briefly dissolving the boundary between human and avian life.

Yet these transformations are haunted by environmental damage. Human despair, when joined with sustained attention to polluted and wounded waters, can become a means of imagining the birds’ own experiences. By looking closely at the habitats they inhabit and the threats they endure, people may begin to understand not only the vulnerability of water birds but also their resilience—their capacity to survive, adapt, and persist in landscapes altered by human desire.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores humanity’s imaginative identification with darters, birds whose lives unfold at the uncertain boundary between water and air. Through surreal transformations, the distinction between human observer and bird gradually dissolves: people seem to enter the darters’ bodies, share their movements, and experience the world through their precarious forms. Artistic observation becomes a means of crossing this boundary, allowing the speaker not merely to describe the birds but to recognize in them familiar emotions and vulnerabilities. Images of fishing, love, captivity, and ecological ruin connect their existence to human desire, dependence, and violence. The birds are therefore both living creatures and symbolic figures, caught within damaged environments shaped by human activity.

This identification becomes especially powerful when the poem turns toward personal despair. Suffering does not isolate the speaker completely; instead, it creates a deeper sensitivity to the birds’ struggle for survival. Their wet, burdened, or struggling wings reflect emotional exhaustion, yet their continued effort also embodies endurance. In this way, the darters become symbols of resilience without being reduced to simple emblems of hope. Their persistence remains fragile and uncertain, threatened by captivity, exploitation, and environmental destruction. By bringing private grief into contact with ecological devastation, the poem suggests that human and nonhuman suffering are inseparable. Its imaginative transformations ultimately invite readers to see empathy as an act of recognition: to perceive in the birds’ damaged world both the consequences of human actions and the possibility of continuing to live, move, and resist amid ruin.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem about darters, fishermen, lovers, and environmental despair, ending with the image of wet wings working the tide.
counterfactuals.output:
Darters stitch black commas  
through the river’s unfinished sentence,  
their necks slick with oil-light,  
their eyes two drowned suns.

On the bank, fishermen cast  
their thin questions into green silence.  
Hooks descend like little moons  
seeking mouths that remember hunger.

The lovers lie beneath a dead willow,  
sharing an orange peeled like weather.  
They whisper of leaving,  
though every road has grown gills  
and every city coughs in its sleep.

Upstream, factories bloom—  
iron flowers exhaling winter.  
Plastic bags drift among reeds,  
pale jellyfish of our convenience,  
while the river carries its fever  
toward an ocean already dreaming  
of deserts.

One fisherman pulls up a shoe.  
Another, a silver fish  
with a bottle cap for a heart.  
Nobody laughs.

At dusk the darters rise,  
ragged priests from the poisoned shallows,  
opening their bodies to the storm.  
The lovers hold each other  
as if touch could dam the dark,  
as if sorrow were only water  
and water could still forgive—

above them, against the ruined horizon,  
wet wings working the tide.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental ecopoem in which water birds emerge from human imagination, become symbols for sailors and artists, and blur the boundary between people and birds.
counterfactuals.output:
**Field Guide to the Imagined Estuary**

At first there was no heron—  
only a long thought standing  
ankle-deep in the skull.

We gave it reeds.  
We gave it a silver grammar of minnows.  
It opened one impossible wing  
and the marsh remembered itself.

Then gulls spilled from sailors’ mouths,  
white knots tied above the mast,  
each cry a compass needle  
trembling toward weather.

*Follow us,* they said,  
or perhaps the wind said it  
through their hollow bones.

On shore, painters mixed dusk  
with oil, feather, salt—  
dabbed cormorants onto the horizon  
until black strokes climbed from the canvas  
and hung their wet wings  
over the sun.

Who made whom?

The artist’s wrist bends like a neck.  
The deckhand sleeps with one eye  
on the moonlit shoal.  
Under his tongue, a tern  
keeps turning north.

Meanwhile the estuary enters us:  
brackish blood, tidal lungs,  
plastic brightening the nest  
like a bad idea we cannot stop imagining.

We walk home on two thin legs,  
startled by our shadows.  
We roost in apartment windows.  
We preen rain from each other’s hair.  
Someone calls a human name—

a flock rises.

For one breath  
the sky is crowded with faces,  
the faces feathered with sky,

and every body—  
sailor, ibis, painter, child—  
is only water  
learning how to leave the water,

only water  
dreaming it has wings.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, dreamlike poem about anhingas or darters that includes Key Largo, brackish estuaries, iridescent plumage, dead bodies of water, and the nightly news.
counterfactuals.output:
**Darter Nocturne**

In Key Largo, dusk unbuttons the mangroves,  
and anhingas rise from brackish estuaries  
like black thoughts the moon has tried to drown.

Their iridescent plumage keeps the last light—  
oil-slick green, bruised violet,  
a secret weather trembling on each wing.

They spear the tide, then surface slowly,  
serpent-necked, carrying silver in their beaks  
through dead bodies of water  
where drowned stars gather without names.

On the nightly news, another shore is burning.  
The anchor’s mouth opens and closes soundlessly  
behind the motel bar, while outside  
the darters crucify themselves to dry—

wings spread against the humid dark,  
each bird a torn umbrella,  
each feather shining as if death, too,  
dreamed of becoming beautiful.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary prose poem exploring humanity’s desire to imitate water birds, combining ornithology, transformation, ecological grief, and bitter humor. Avoid rhyme and use vivid surreal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
We have always wanted the bodies of water birds: the grebe’s hinged feet, the loon’s dense bones, the cormorant’s black apparatus lowering itself through the lake as if darkness had learned to hunt. Instead, we invented swim fins, waterproof mascara, and vacation photographs in which everyone pretends not to be cold. We enter the shallows with our phones held overhead like frightened gods.

At the marsh, a heron folds the afternoon into its neck. Its patience humiliates us. We have built observation decks, binoculars, interpretive signs explaining that the animal before us is alive. Nearby, a mallard drags an oil rainbow through the reeds, iridescent as a corporate apology. The chicks follow, small commas in a sentence the century refuses to finish.

Some nights I dream my shoulder blades split and release two wet wings. My teeth soften into a bill. My lungs revise their contract. I dive beneath the reservoir and find the drowned town still lit: traffic signals changing for catfish, a school bus furred with algae, refrigerators opening their white mouths to silt. I perch on the steeple and preen microplastics from my new breast. Transformation, it turns out, includes maintenance.

The ornithologists say the loon cannot walk well on land, its legs set far back for propulsion. We admire this specialization while designing airports on wetlands. We call the result progress because “catastrophic habitat conversion” does not fit on a ribbon-cutting banner. Above us, geese draft one another through exhausted air, each bird borrowing lift from the wound ahead.

Still, at the municipal pond, we practice. We extend our arms. We flap beside warning signs and vending machines. Children do it sincerely; adults do it after cocktails. For one ridiculous second, the species leans toward another possibility. Then the gulls rise from the landfill, carrying our wrappers like bright entrails, and we applaud—as if they have performed for us, as if applause were not the smallest sound a pair of useless wings can make.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine fishermen, painters, ornithologists, and lovers confronting darters in a climate-damaged coastal world. Turn the scenario into a lyrical free-verse poem about creation, despair, and identification with nonhuman life.
counterfactuals.output:
After the sea climbed the chapel steps  
and taught salt to the wheat,  
the fishermen came inland  
carrying nets like torn constellations.

They found the darters in drowned cypress—  
black necks unspooling from the glare,  
wings opened to the poisoned sun  
as if drying the pages of a ruined book.

Painters mixed ash with ultramarine,  
rust with the green of storm drains.  
They tried to make the birds appear  
without making them beautiful,

but beauty kept leaking through:  
the needle-beak, the wet silk body,  
the sudden silver fish  
briefly stitched between hunger and air.

Ornithologists whispered old names  
over tablets warm as fever:  
snakebird, water-turkey, anhinga—  
each word a small raft,  
each measurement another way  
to say, Stay.

And the lovers, who had nowhere left  
that was not forecast or floodplain,  
lay beneath the mangroves listening  
to generators fail one by one.

They watched two darters rise  
from the refinery marsh,  
their shadows crossing the moon’s  
oil-bright face.

We made this, one lover said—  
meaning the broken seawall,  
the plastic flowering in the wrack,  
the sky with its red machinery.

We made this, said the other—  
meaning the kiss,  
the names for every vanishing thing,  
the painted bird lifting  
from a human hand.

At dawn the fishermen entered the water  
until water entered them.  
The painters darkened their own arms  
with wings.  
The ornithologists forgot  
which side of the glass  
they had been studying.

All of us stood with our backs  
to the terrible light,  
holding them open.

All of us waited for wind  
to pass through our feathers.

All of us, narrow-necked and starving,  
looked down into the changed sea  
and recognized our bright prey,  
our bright grief,

then plunged.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
